fetched_contents.text: HIV Treatment and care in children and adolescents An estimated 1.4 million children aged 0-14 were living with HIV at the end of 2023, and 120 000 children were newly infected. An estimated 76 000 children died of AIDS-related illnesses. To reduce HIV-related mortality and morbidity among this highly vulnerable population, early testing and treatment is essential. Without access to testing and treatment, 50% of children with HIV will die by the age of 2, and 80% will not live to their fifth birthday. WHO recommends that infants born to mothers living with HIV are tested for HIV by two months of age, during breastfeeding, and when breastfeeding ends given continued risk of transmission during this period. Older children, especially offspring and siblings of persons infected with HIV, should also be tested in high prevalence regions. Community-based outreach and testing can improve access to testing while mitigating HIV-related stigma. Children living with HIV should start antiretroviral treatment (ART) immediately. Yet in 2023, only 57% of children were on ART, compared to 77% of adults. Once treatment begins, children must take their medicine regularly to stay healthy into adolescence and adulthood. Failure to suppress the HIV virus remains a serious problem among children, aggravated by a lack of child-friendly formulations of the newest and most effective antiretroviral drugs designed for adults. Globally in 2023, an estimated 1.5 million adolescents (10-19 years old) were living with HIV and an estimated 140 000 were newly infected with HIV. Compared to other populations, adolescents face additional barriers in accessing testing and treatment, including health services that are not adapted to their needs and policies that require parental consent for services. Adolescents living with HIV are also less likely than adults to adhere to their treatment, resulting in lower rates of viral suppression and lower declines in mortality. Addressing the distinct and diverse needs of adolescents living with HIV to improve their HIV-related outcomes requires a comprehensive and integrated approach that leverages on global commitments and approaches to adolescent health, including the Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030) and the Global Accelerated Action for the Health of Adolescents (AA-HA!). WHO recommends the implementation of adolescent-friendly health services in HIV services to ensure engagement and improved outcomes. Involving and engaging in their own care across the treatment cascade and through the cycle of planning, implementing, monitoring and evaluating programs is key. Peer-driven, adolescent-friendly services, integrated with other services including psychosocial interventions, are effective ways to improve health outcomes for adolescents. fetched_contents.text: Initiation of Antiretroviral Therapy in Children with HIV Infection When to Initiate Antiretroviral Treatment in Children With HIV Infection Updated September 30, 2025 Reviewed September 30, 2025 Panel’s Recommendations * Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all infants and children with HIV infection (AI for children aged <3 months, AI* for older children). * Rapid ART initiation (defined as initiating ART immediately or within days of HIV diagnosis), accompanied by a discussion of the importance of adherence and provision of subsequent adherence support, is recommended for all children with HIV (AI*). * However, in ART-naive children and adolescents with cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease, the Panel on Antiretroviral Therapy and Medical Management of Children Living With HIV recommends initiation of treatment for the opportunistic infection first, before ART initiation (see Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in Children With and Exposed to HIV) (AII). The timing of ART initiation in these cases should be discussed with a pediatric HIV specialist. * If a child with HIV has not initiated ART, health care providers should closely monitor the virologic, immunologic, and clinical status at least every 3 to 4 months (AIII). * ART initiation should be discussed and strongly encouraged at every visit (AIII). Rating of Recommendations: A = Strong; B = Moderate; C = Optional Rating of Evidence: I = One or more randomized trials in children† with clinical outcomes and/or validated endpoints; I* = One or more randomized trials in adults with clinical outcomes and/or validated laboratory endpoints with accompanying data in children† from one or more well-designed, nonrandomized trials or observational cohort studies with long-term clinical outcomes; II = One or more well-designed, nonrandomized trials or observational cohort studies in children† with long-term outcomes; II* = One or more well-designed, nonrandomized trials or observational studies in adults with long-term clinical outcomes with accompanying data in children† from one or more similar nonrandomized trials or cohort studies with clinical outcome data; III = Expert opinion †Studies that include children or children/adolescents, but not studies limited to postpubertal adolescents Overview The Panel on Antiretroviral Therapy and Medical Management of Children Living With HIV (the Panel) recommends initiating treatment for all children with HIV as soon as is feasible after diagnosis. Multiple studies have shown a benefit to early antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation1-3 and that ART initiation within the first year of life is associated with reduced size of viral reservoirs.4 Treatment initiation in young infants with HIV during the early stages of infection may control viral replication before HIV can evolve into diverse and potentially more pathogenic quasi-species.5 Initiation of therapy at higher CD4 T lymphocyte (CD4) cell counts has been associated with the presence of fewer drug-resistant mutations at virologic failure in adults.6 Early therapy has also been shown to preserve immune function and prevent clinical disease progression in perinatal infection7-9 and may prevent or reduce persistent inflammation, a precipitant of cardiovascular, kidney, and liver disease and malignancy.10,11 Rapid treatment initiation, defined as therapy initiated immediately or within days of HIV diagnosis, is recommended except in children with cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease. Due to concerns regarding the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, ART initiation may be deferred briefly until the optimal timing relative to treatment of these opportunistic infections. Timing of ART initiation in these cases should be discussed with a pediatric HIV specialist (see Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in Children With and Exposed to HIV). A retrospective review of children and adolescents with HIV in six African countries between 2013 and 2020 showed that there was no mortality difference if ART was initiated <2 weeks (n = 266) versus 2 weeks to 2 months (n = 398) after starting anti-tuberculous therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis (TB).12 This finding supporting ART initiation in children and adolescents with HIV within the first 2 weeks of treatment for TB is consistent with World Health Organization Updated Recommendations on HIV Prevention, Infant Diagnosis, Antiretroviral Initiation and Monitoring, March 2021,13 which advocate for ART initiation within 2 weeks of TB treatment initiation for infants and children, except when signs and symptoms of meningitis are present. . In the case of tuberculous meningitis, the Panel recommends initiating ART within 2 to 8 weeks of TB treatment initiation, depending on clinical considerations and in consultation with a pediatric HIV specialist (see Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in Children With and Exposed to HIV). Although rapid initiation of ART is recommended in all children with HIV, individual clinical and/or psychosocial factors may lead patients, caregivers, and providers to make a collaborative decision to defer ART initiation. When making the decision to defer ART, medical factors—such as the opportunity to limit seeding of the viral reservoir in newborns, the child’s HIV disease stage,14 and the presence of HIV-related signs and symptoms15—need to be balanced against any potential barriers to rapid ART initiation. If ART is deferred, the health care provider should continue to educate and work with the family to overcome barriers to treatment, as well as closely monitor the child’s virologic, immunologic, and clinical status at least every 3 to 4 months; more frequent monitoring may be needed in infants or young children ≤4 years of…

fetched_contents.text: Understanding Antiretroviral Therapy Adherence in Children With HIV: A Review of Barriers and Strategies Abstract Introduction Despite advancements in antiretroviral therapy (ART) availability, maintaining optimal adherence remains difficult, especially in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs). This literature review synthesized evidence on barriers and interventions influencing adherence to ART among children and adolescents with HIV, focusing on studies conducted in LMICs, particularly in Africa and Asia, where adherence and challenges are more prevalent. Methods This narrative review draws on peer‐reviewed studies to identify barriers to ART adherence, such as medication complexity, caregiver‐related issues, socioeconomic factors, and healthcare infrastructure limitations. A thorough search was conducted using electronic databases like PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus, covering relevant primary and secondary literature from 2010 to 2023 in LMICs in Africa and Asia. It also evaluates the effectiveness of digital tools and psychosocial interventions in enhancing adherence to ART among children with HIV. Results and Discussion Findings reveal that adherence remains suboptimal, with rates ranging from 62% to 95% across settings. Major barriers include regimen complexity, psychosocial stressors, and limited healthcare access, while interventions such as digital adherence tools, caregiver education, and community‐based programs demonstrate measurable improvements. Evidence highlights that targeted interventions can improve outcomes. Family support programs in Uganda increased adherence from 66% to 83%, and SMS reminder systems improved adherence by up to 5.5% among adolescents. Nevertheless, recent reductions in international funding pose a substantial threat to the sustainability of these gains in resource‐limited settings. Conclusion Improving adherence among children and adolescents requires not only simplified regimens and psychosocial support but also sustainable financing mechanisms. Future strategies must anticipate barriers related to funding cuts, drug resistance, and the transition from pediatric to adult care. As of 2023, an estimated 2.38 million children aged 0–18 were living with HIV worldwide, highlighting the ongoing need for effective treatment and care [3]. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has been crucial in improving health outcomes for people living with HIV, including children populations, by reducing morbidity and mortality rates [4]. However, achieving optimal adherence to the ART regimen remains a significant challenge, which is necessary to control the virus and prevent drug resistance, which could lead to treatment failure [5, 6]. Despite improvements in ART availability, only about 57% of children aged 0–14 living with HIV received treatment in 2023, leaving many children at risk of disease progression [1]. Additionally, about 685 new HIV infections are reported in children each day, and approximately 250 children die daily from AIDS‐related causes [3]. These statistics show the urgent need for strategies that not only increase ART coverage but also focus on improving adherence, especially in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs) where the burden is highest. One key difference between children and adults living with HIV is that children rely heavily on their caregivers for treatment adherence [4]. Unlike adults, children cannot manage their medication on their own, meaning that parents, guardians, or healthcare providers play a crucial role in ensuring they take their medication regularly. Caregivers are responsible for managing daily doses, handling side effects, and navigating healthcare systems [7]. The mental health, social support, and knowledge of these caregivers can directly impact how well children adhere to ART [7]. In many low‐resource settings, caregivers face additional challenges such as stigma, lack of healthcare access, and financial struggles, which can further hinder adherence [8, 9]. New digital tools, like mobile health apps, electronic medication reminders, and telemedicine, have shown potential in helping children and their caregivers stick to ART, particularly in high‐resource settings [11, 12]. These technologies offer real‐time monitoring and reminders, which can help both children and caregivers manage treatment more effectively [11]. WHO’s guidelines for ART initiation in children are meant to support broader global health targets centered on universal access, viral suppression, and elimination of HIV-related mortality, especially among children and adolescents. The most directly relevant target framework is the 90-90-90 and 95-95-95 targets, which are referenced in the UNAIDS evidence set as targets aiming to bring HIV testing and treatment to the majority of people living with HIV by 2020 and later to support ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5]. UNAIDS’s 2030 targets also emphasize reducing new HIV infections and related mortality, which aligns with the broader goal of expanding ART coverage and early treatment to children [N3-R2]. WHO’s child HIV treatment guidance explicitly states that every child and adolescent living with HIV should have access to antiretroviral therapy (ART), and that early testing and treatment is essential to reduce HIV-related mortality and morbidity [N1-F1]. This means child ART is directly tied to meeting the 90-90-90/95-95-95 targets by increasing the proportion of children who know their status, are on treatment, and achieve viral suppression [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R4].

Early ART initiation supports these targets through several mechanisms. First, it improves viral suppression, which is a core requirement of the 90-90-90/95-95-95 framework. WHO emphasizes that children should start ART immediately after diagnosis, and that rapid initiation within the first few days of life has been associated with faster CD4 recovery and reduced viral reservoir size [N4-F2][N2-R4]. Second, early initiation helps preserve immune function and prevents clinical disease progression, which in turn supports retention in care and long-term survival [N4-F2]. Third, the evidence cited in the NIH guidance indicates that ART initiation within the first year of life is associated with reduced size of viral reservoirs, and that early therapy has been shown to preserve immune function and prevent clinical disease progression in perinatal infection [N4-F2]. This directly supports the target of reducing AIDS-related mortality among children, which WHO notes is still very high: an estimated 76,000 children died of AIDS-related illnesses in 2023 [N1-F1].

The guidelines also align closely with UNAIDS and WHO global treatment targets. WHO’s treatment-and-care page states that children and adolescents should start ART immediately and that adolescents face additional barriers in accessing testing and treatment, including services not adapted to their needs and policies requiring parental consent [N1-F1]. This aligns with the UNAIDS “START FREE, STAY FREE, AIDS FREE” initiative and broader global commitments to adolescent-friendly services and access to lifelong ART [N1-F1]. The global HIV targets described in UNAIDS’s 2030 recommendations include reducing new HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths, which are precisely the outcomes that early ART helps achieve [N3-R2][N3-R5]. WHO’s 2021 guidelines also promote the use of optimal ART regimens in all populations and emphasize that early ART initiation is recommended except in special cases such as cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease [N4-F2]. This reflects a broader global treatment target of minimizing treatment delays and maximizing treatment coverage while carefully managing complex clinical situations [N4-F2].

In short, the child ART guidelines support the 90-90-90/95-95-95 targets by increasing testing, treatment initiation, and viral suppression, and they support UNAIDS and WHO global targets by reducing new infections, AIDS-related mortality, and disparities in access and retention [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N4-F2].

The changes in child ART guidance have been implemented with the expectation that early treatment will improve outcomes, but implementation barriers and evidence gaps remain substantial, especially in low-resource settings. One major barrier is adherence, which is central to treatment success. The NIH evidence on adherence notes that suboptimal adherence may include missed or late doses, and that adherence is a principal determinant of virologic suppression [N5-F3]. In low- and middle-income countries, adherence is further complicated by regimen complexity, psychosocial stressors, limited healthcare access, and caregiver-related challenges [N5-F3]. The NIH evidence also highlights that children rely heavily on caregivers for treatment adherence, and that caregiver mental health, social support, and knowledge can directly impact children’s adherence [N5-F3]. In many low-resource settings, caregivers face stigma, lack of healthcare access, and financial struggles, which can further hinder adherence [N5-F3]. These factors explain why only 57% of children living with HIV were on ART globally in 2023, compared to 77% of adults [N1-F1].

Implementation also differs across regions and health systems. WHO explicitly states that adolescents and young adults aged 10–24 remain underserved in the global HIV response, and that adolescents face additional barriers such as services not adapted to their needs and policies requiring parental consent [N1-F1]. Adolescents are also less likely than adults to adhere to treatment, resulting in lower rates of viral suppression and lower declines in mortality [N1-F1]. The evidence on adherence also notes that interventions such as digital adherence tools, caregiver education, and community-based programs can improve outcomes, but recent reductions in international funding threaten the sustainability of these gains [N5-F3]. This suggests that implementation effectiveness is highly dependent on local infrastructure, financing, and program design, and that what works in high-resource settings may not scale easily in low-resource settings.

Ongoing monitoring and follow-up remain a key recommendation. WHO’s guidance states that ART initiation should be discussed and strongly encouraged at every visit, and that health care providers should closely monitor virologic, immunologic, and clinical status at least every 3 to 4 months [N4-F2]. The NIH evidence also notes that baseline CD4 count and age at ART initiation affect how rapidly CD4 count improves after ART initiation [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This means that monitoring is not merely administrative but clinically meaningful, and that follow-up must be tailored to individual patient characteristics. The NIH evidence further highlights that early ART initiation within the first 7 days of life compared with initiation between 8 and 28 days of life resulted in a fourfold faster increase in CD4 count, underscoring the importance of close post-initiation monitoring [N2-R4]. Overall, the guidance emphasizes that early treatment must be followed by sustained monitoring and support to maintain viral suppression and prevent disease progression [N4-F2][N5-F3].

In summary, the changes have been implemented with the expectation of improved outcomes, but low-resource settings face major barriers including adherence, caregiver burden, stigma, and limited healthcare access [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Practice varies across regions and health systems, particularly around adolescent-friendly services, parental consent, and service adaptation [N1-F1]. Ongoing monitoring and follow-up remain essential, especially for virologic, immunologic, and clinical status, with follow-up frequency and intensity adjusted according to age and clinical context [N4-F2][N2-R1][N2-R3].

This means the threshold became less restrictive in general, because treatment is no longer deferred unless there are specific clinical indications for delay. In contrast, older guidance would have been more conditional on CD4 count, viral load, or age, but the latest evidence suggests that early initiation is preferred [N4-F2]. The WHO treatment-and-care page also states that children living with HIV should start ART immediately, which reinforces the shift toward immediate initiation [N1-F1].

Age is treated as a critical factor in the latest guidelines, but the threshold is not tied to a specific cutoff age. Instead, the guidance emphasizes that ART should be initiated as soon as is feasible after diagnosis, and that rapid initiation within the first few days of life has been associated with faster CD4 recovery and reduced viral reservoir size [N4-F2][N2-R4]. The NIH evidence also notes that baseline CD4 count and age at ART initiation affect how rapidly CD4 count improves after ART initiation [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This means age is used as a modifier of expected outcomes, not as a strict eligibility criterion. Similarly, weight is not explicitly mentioned as a defining eligibility threshold in the provided evidence, but weight-related practical considerations are likely relevant in dose selection and regimen choice, which are part of treatment readiness rather than the initiation decision itself.

CD4 count is treated as an important clinical determinant, but the guidelines do not set a fixed cutpoint for initiation. The NIH evidence says that ART initiation within the first year of life is associated with reduced viral reservoir size and that early therapy has been shown to preserve immune function and prevent clinical disease progression in perinatal infection [N4-F2]. It also notes that initiation at higher CD4 T lymphocyte (CD4) cell counts has been associated with fewer drug-resistant mutations at virologic failure in adults, and that early therapy helps preserve immune function [N4-F2]. In the provided evidence, CD4 count is therefore used to inform timing and expected outcomes, but the threshold for initiating treatment remains low and immediate [N4-F2][N2-R1][N2-R3]. Viral load is not explicitly stated as a separate eligibility criterion in the evidence provided, but early initiation is supported by the idea that early therapy controls viral replication before HIV can evolve into more pathogenic quasi-species [N4-F2]. In other words, viral load is part of the clinical rationale for early treatment, but not a standalone threshold.

Treatment readiness and pre-treatment staging are also addressed, though the evidence is more about the timing of initiation than a formal staging system. The guidelines emphasize that ART initiation should be discussed and strongly encouraged at every visit, and that health care providers should closely monitor virologic, immunologic, and clinical status at least every 3 to 4 months [N4-F2]. They also note that in ART-naive children and adolescents with opportunistic infections such as cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease, treatment for the opportunistic infection should be initiated first before ART initiation, and timing should be discussed with a pediatric HIV specialist [N4-F2]. The evidence also says that individual clinical and/or psychosocial factors may lead to a collaborative decision to defer ART initiation, balancing the opportunity to limit seeding of the viral reservoir with potential barriers to rapid initiation [N4-F2].

In conclusion, the WHO guidelines have moved toward more immediate initiation, with the threshold becoming less restrictive in general but more conditional in special clinical cases. Age is treated as a modifier of outcomes rather than a fixed eligibility cutoff, CD4 count is used to inform expected response and timing, and viral load is part of the clinical rationale for early treatment. Pre-treatment staging remains important, especially for opportunistic infections, but is managed through clinical judgment and specialist consultation rather than a separate staging system [N4-F2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N1-F1].

WHO’s treatment-and-care page also states that children living with HIV should start ART immediately, reinforcing the move toward immediate initiation [N1-F1]. The evidence further supports this by showing that early initiation within the first 7 days of life compared with initiation between 8 and 28 days of life resulted in a fourfold faster increase in CD4 count [N2-R4].

Age is treated as a **modifier of expected outcomes**, not a fixed eligibility cutoff. The guidelines emphasize that ART should be initiated as soon as is feasible after diagnosis and that rapid initiation within the first few days of life has been associated with faster CD4 recovery and reduced viral reservoir size [N4-F2][N2-R4]. Baseline CD4 count and age at ART initiation also affect how rapidly CD4 count improves after ART initiation, indicating that CD4 count is used to inform timing and expected response rather than to set a strict threshold [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Viral load is part of the clinical rationale for early treatment, but it is not presented as a standalone eligibility criterion in the provided evidence [N4-F2].

Treatment readiness and pre-treatment staging remain important, but they are handled through **clinical prioritization rather than a rigid staging system**. In children with opportunistic infections such as cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease, treatment for the opportunistic infection should be initiated first before ART initiation, and timing should be discussed with a pediatric HIV specialist [N4-F2]. This means that pre-treatment staging is still important, but it is conditional on clinical judgment and specialist consultation rather than a separate algorithm. The evidence also notes that individual clinical and/or psychosocial factors may lead to a collaborative decision to defer ART initiation, balancing the opportunity to limit seeding of the viral reservoir with potential barriers to rapid initiation [N4-F2].

### 2. What global health targets the guidelines aim to support

The WHO guidelines are meant to support broader global health targets centered on **universal access, viral suppression, and elimination of HIV-related mortality**, especially among children and adolescents [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R5]. The most directly relevant target framework is the **90-90-90 and 95-95-95 targets**, which are referenced in the UNAIDS evidence set as targets aimed at bringing HIV testing and treatment to the majority of people living with HIV [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5]. UNAIDS’s 2030 targets also emphasize reducing new HIV infections and related mortality, which aligns with the broader goal of expanding ART coverage and early treatment to children [N3-R2].

Child ART contributes to these targets in several ways. First, it increases the proportion of children who know their status, are on treatment, and achieve viral suppression, which is central to the 90-90-90/95-95-95 framework [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R4]. Second, early ART initiation supports **viral suppression, retention, and mortality reduction**. The evidence shows that early initiation improves CD4 recovery, reduces viral reservoir size, preserves immune function, and prevents clinical disease progression in perinatal infection [N4-F2][N2-R4]. WHO’s guidance also states that children should start ART immediately because early testing and treatment is essential to reduce HIV-related mortality and morbidity [N1-F1]. This is important because WHO notes that an estimated 76,000 children died of AIDS-related illnesses in 2023 [N1-F1].

The guidelines also align closely with **UNAIDS and WHO global treatment targets**. WHO explicitly states that every child and adolescent living with HIV should have access to antiretroviral therapy (ART), and that adolescents face additional barriers in accessing testing and treatment, including services not adapted to their needs and policies requiring parental consent [N1-F1]. This aligns with the “START FREE, STAY FREE, AIDS FREE” initiative and broader global commitments to adolescent-friendly services and lifelong ART [N1-F1]. WHO’s 2021 guidelines also promote the use of optimal ART regimens in all populations and emphasize that early ART initiation is recommended except in special cases [N4-F2]. This reflects a broader global treatment target of minimizing treatment delays and maximizing treatment coverage while carefully managing complex clinical situations [N4-F2].

### 3. How the changes have been implemented and what remains uncertain

The changes have been implemented with the expectation that early treatment will improve outcomes, but **implementation barriers and evidence gaps remain substantial**, especially in low-resource settings [N1-F1][N5-F3]. One major barrier is **adherence**, which is central to treatment success. The NIH evidence notes that suboptimal adherence may include missed or late doses, and that adherence is a principal determinant of virologic suppression [N5-F3]. In low- and middle-income countries, adherence is further complicated by regimen complexity, psychosocial stressors, limited healthcare access, and caregiver-related challenges [N5-F3]. The evidence also highlights that children rely heavily on caregivers for treatment adherence, and that caregiver mental health, social support, and knowledge can directly impact children’s adherence [N5-F3]. In many low-resource settings, caregivers face stigma, lack of healthcare access, and financial struggles, which can further hinder adherence [N5-F3].

Implementation also differs across **regions and health systems**. WHO states that adolescents and young adults aged 10–24 remain underserved in the global HIV response, and that adolescents face additional barriers such as services not adapted to their needs and policies requiring parental consent [N1-F1]. Adolescents are also less likely than adults to adhere to treatment, resulting in lower rates of viral suppression and lower declines in mortality [N1-F1]. The evidence on adherence also notes that interventions such as digital adherence tools, caregiver education, and community-based programs can improve outcomes, but recent reductions in international funding threaten the sustainability of these gains [N5-F3]. This suggests that implementation effectiveness is highly dependent on local infrastructure, financing, and program design, and that what works in high-resource settings may not scale easily in low-resource settings.

Ongoing monitoring and follow-up remain a key recommendation. WHO’s guidance states that ART initiation should be discussed and strongly encouraged at every visit, and that health care providers should closely monitor virologic, immunologic, and clinical status at least every 3 to 4 months [N4-F2]. The NIH evidence also notes that baseline CD4 count and age at ART initiation affect how rapidly CD4 count improves after ART initiation [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This means that monitoring is not merely administrative but clinically meaningful, and that follow-up must be tailored to individual patient characteristics. The NIH evidence further highlights that early ART initiation within the first 7 days of life compared with initiation between 8 and 28 days of life resulted in a fourfold faster increase in CD4 count, underscoring the importance of close post-initiation monitoring [N2-R4]. Overall, the guidance emphasizes that early treatment must be followed by sustained monitoring and support to maintain viral suppression and prevent disease progression [N4-F2][N5-F3].

### 4. How WHO’s current guidance differs from older guidance and where evidence is strongest

WHO’s current child ART guidance differs from older guidance in three main ways: the threshold for initiation has become more immediate, the evidence base for early treatment is stronger, and some recommendations remain conditional or pending further evidence [N4-F2][N1-F1]. The latest guidance recommends initiating treatment for all children with HIV as soon as is feasible after diagnosis, and that rapid initiation is recommended for all children with HIV except in special clinical cases [N4-F2]. This is a shift from older guidance, which may have relied more heavily on CD4 count or age as eligibility criteria [N4-F2]. WHO’s treatment-and-care page also states that children living with HIV should start ART immediately, reinforcing the move toward immediate initiation [N1-F1].

The **strongest evidence** is for **early initiation in infants and young children**. The NIH evidence reports that rapid initiation within the first 7 days of life compared with initiation between 8 and 28 days of life resulted in a fourfold faster increase in CD4 count, and that early initiation within the first year of life is associated with reduced viral reservoir size [N4-F2][N2-R4]. It also states that early therapy has been shown to preserve immune function and prevent clinical disease progression in perinatal infection [N4-F2]. These findings are strong because they are supported by longitudinal cohort data and clinical outcomes rather than weaker observational or expert opinion. The evidence cited in the NIH guidance also indicates that initiation at higher CD4 cell counts has been associated with fewer drug-resistant mutations at virologic failure in adults, and that early therapy helps preserve immune function [N4-F2]. While these adult findings are not direct evidence for children, they are used as supporting evidence alongside child-specific data, which strengthens the overall recommendation for early initiation [N4-F2].

Where evidence is weaker or pending, the guidance remains **conditional or pending further evidence**. First, the NIH evidence notes that individual clinical and/or psychosocial factors may lead to a collaborative decision to defer ART initiation [N4-F2]. This means that while the default recommendation is rapid initiation, exceptions are allowed when there are medical or psychosocial reasons for delay. Second, the evidence for some special cases is conditional on clinical judgment and specialist consultation. For example, the NIH guidance states that ART should be initiated for opportunistic infections first before ART initiation in children with cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease, and timing should be discussed with a pediatric HIV specialist [N4-F2]. This indicates that while the general recommendation is immediate initiation, these special cases require careful clinical evaluation rather than a fixed rule. Finally, the guidance on adolescents notes that adolescents face additional barriers to testing and treatment, including services not adapted to their needs and policies requiring parental consent, and that they are less likely than adults to adhere to treatment [N1-F1]. While the evidence on adolescents is strong in showing the burden and barriers, it does not yet fully resolve how to optimize adolescent-specific initiation and retention in all settings, which remains an area where implementation evidence is still being built [N1-F1].

### 5. Bottom line

In short, WHO’s child ART guidelines have changed since 2013 by making **ART initiation more immediate and less conditional**, with a strong emphasis on early treatment for infants and young children [N4-F2][N1-F1]. The guidelines are meant to support global targets such as **90-90-90/95-95-95**, **reducing new HIV infections**, and **reducing AIDS-related mortality and disparities in access and retention** [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R2][N1-F1]. Implementation has improved, but **low-resource settings still face major barriers including adherence, caregiver burden, stigma, and limited healthcare access**, and practice varies across regions and health systems [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence base is strongest for early initiation in infants, but some recommendations remain conditional or pending further evidence, especially in special cases and adolescent-specific settings [N4-F2][N1-F1].
